title: Liver Disorders and Rh Isoimmunization in Pregnancy

units.title: HELLP Syndrome & Differential Diagnosis of Liver Disorders
units.guide: HELLP syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets) occurs in 10-20% of severe pre-eclampsia cases, typically presenting with right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Tennessee diagnostic criteria require microangiopathic hemolysis (schistocytes, LDH >=600 IU/L, bilirubin >=1.2 mg/dL), AST/ALT elevated at least 2-fold (>=70 IU/L), and platelet count <100,000/microL; serum alkaline phosphatase is excluded as it is physiologically elevated from placental production.

units.title: Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy & Swansea Diagnostic Criteria
units.guide: AFLP is an obstetric emergency caused by fetal homozygous deficiency in long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCHAD) in a heterozygous mother, leading to toxic maternal accumulation of fetal fatty acid intermediates. Presenting in the third trimester with nausea, vomiting, profound hypoglycemia (<72 mg/dL), encephalopathy, and DIC, it is diagnosed via Swansea criteria (>=6 features); prompt maternal stabilization and immediate delivery are lifesaving.

units.title: Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy & Fetal Bile Toxicity
units.guide: ICP is characterized by intractable maternal pruritus primarily affecting palms and soles without primary dermatological rash, worsening nocturnally due to impaired estrogen/progesterone-mediated bile acid excretion. Elevated maternal serum total bile acids (>10 micromol/L) cross into amniotic fluid, irritating fetal bowel (meconium passage), depressing cardiac pacemaker conductance, and risking sudden stillbirth; managed with Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and planned delivery at 36-37 weeks.

units.title: Rh Antigens, Genetics & Isoimmunization Pathophysiology
units.guide: Rh blood group antigens (D, C, c, E, e) are transmembrane proteins encoded by RHD and RHCE genes located on the short arm of chromosome 1 (1p36). The D antigen is by far the most immunogenic; primary fetomaternal hemorrhage sensitizes an Rh-negative mother, initially triggering IgM antibodies (which cannot cross the placenta), followed post-delivery or in secondary exposures by maternal IgG anti-D which freely cross the placenta to destroy Rh-positive fetal red cells.

units.title: Rh Isoimmunization: Fetal Anemia & Hydrops Fetalis
units.guide: Maternal IgG anti-D binding causes extravascular splenic destruction of fetal red blood cells, resulting in fetal anemia and compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis in liver and spleen. When fetal hematocrit falls below 15% (Hb <4 g/dL), high-output heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, and capillary leakage trigger Hydrops Fetalis (defined by fluid accumulation in >=2 serous compartments: ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, or subcutaneous scalp edema [Buddha sign]).

units.title: Management of Unsensitized Rh-Negative Mother & Anti-D
units.guide: All Rh-negative pregnant women undergo an Indirect Coombs Test (ICT) at booking. If ICT is negative (unsensitized), routine antenatal prophylaxis with 300 mcg (1500 IU) Anti-D immunoglobulin is administered at 28 weeks; following delivery, if the newborn is Rh-positive with a negative Direct Coombs Test (DCT), another 300 mcg dose is administered within 72 hours (up to 28 days), coupled with early cord clamping during delivery.

units.title: Management of Rh-Sensitized Mother: Titer, MCA Doppler & IUT
units.guide: In Rh-sensitized women (ICT positive), maternal antibody titer is monitored; a titer >=1:16 is critical, mandating fetal surveillance for anemia. Middle Cerebral Artery Peak Systolic Velocity (MCA PSV) Doppler is the non-invasive screening gold standard: PSV >=1.5 MoM indicates moderate-to-severe fetal anemia. This is confirmed via cordocentesis (fetal hematocrit <30%), followed by intrauterine blood transfusion (IUT) with O-negative irradiated CMV-negative PRBCs if gestation is <35 weeks.

units.title: Fetomaternal Hemorrhage, Minor Antigens & Mirror Syndrome
units.guide: Excessive fetomaternal hemorrhage (>30 mL whole blood) is screened by the Rosette test and precisely quantified by the Kleihauer-Betke (KB) acid elution test, requiring 10 mcg extra anti-D per 1 mL fetal whole blood over 30 mL. Anti-Kell alloimmunization is the most common non-D cause following mismatched transfusion (causing erythroblast suppression), while Anti-c is the most severe; Mirror syndrome (Ballantyne syndrome) involves maternal generalized edema and hydrops mirroring fetal hydrops.

questions.q: What three classic clinical components define HELLP syndrome, and what is its most common presenting symptom?
opts: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets; presenting most commonly with right upper quadrant or epigastric abdominal pain
Hepatic failure, Encephalopathy, Leukopenia, and Polyuria; presenting with painless jaundice
Hypertension, Edema, Lung lesions, and Proteinuria; presenting with dyspnea
Hyperglycemia, Elevated Lipids, Lactic acidosis, and Pruritus; presenting with intense itching
questions.exp: HELLP denotes microangiopathic Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets; abdominal/epigastric pain is present in up to 90% of cases. (Book p406)

questions.q: According to the Tennessee criteria for HELLP syndrome, which laboratory threshold confirms microangiopathic hemolysis?
opts: Serum LDH >= 600 IU/L, abnormal peripheral smear with schistocytes/burr cells, or total serum bilirubin >= 1.2 mg/dL
questions.exp: Tennessee criteria require evidence of hemolysis: LDH >= 600 IU/L, peripheral schistocytes/burr cells, bilirubin >= 1.2 mg/dL, or low haptoglobin. (Book p406)

questions.q: Why is serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) deliberately EXCLUDED from the diagnostic criteria for HELLP syndrome?
opts: Alkaline phosphatase is physiologically elevated by 2- to 3-fold during normal pregnancy due to placental isoenzyme production
Alkaline phosphatase levels drop to zero in liver failure
Alkaline phosphatase is only produced in the fetal myocardium
Alkaline phosphatase cannot be assayed during pregnancy
questions.exp: Placental syncytiotrophoblasts secrete heat-stable alkaline phosphatase, elevating maternal levels normally and rendering ALP non-specific for liver injury. (Book p406)

questions.q: What platelet count threshold defines thrombocytopenia in complete HELLP syndrome?
questions.exp: Complete HELLP syndrome requires thrombocytopenia with platelets < 100,000/mm3 (Tennessee criteria) or < 50,000 for Class 1 (Mississippi). (Book p406)

questions.q: What catastrophic intra-abdominal hepatic complication can occur in severe pre-eclampsia / HELLP syndrome, presenting with sudden right upper quadrant pain, shoulder pain, and hypovolemic shock?
questions.exp: Subcapsular hepatic hematoma rupture carries high maternal-fetal mortality and requires urgent surgical intervention or embolization. (Book p407)

questions.q: What fetal inborn error of metabolism is causally linked to the development of Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy (AFLP) in a heterozygous mother?
opts: Fetal homozygous deficiency of Long-Chain 3-Hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase (LCHAD)
questions.exp: Homozygous fetal LCHAD enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of fetal long-chain fatty acids that enter maternal circulation and poison the maternal liver. (Book p407)

questions.q: Which metabolic abnormality is a distinctive hallmark that strongly differentiates AFLP from pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome?
opts: Profound maternal hypoglycemia (< 72 mg/dL) due to catastrophic hepatic glycogen depletion and impaired gluconeogenesis
questions.exp: Severe hypoglycemia is a cardinal feature of AFLP distinguishing it from HELLP syndrome and reflecting fulminant hepatic parenchymal failure. (Book p407)

questions.q: What diagnostic consensus criteria are used clinically to establish the diagnosis of Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy without requiring a liver biopsy?
opts: Swansea criteria (presence of 6 or more clinical and laboratory features in the absence of another explanation)
questions.exp: Swansea criteria (requiring >= 6 of 14 features including vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia/polyuria, jaundice, hypoglycemia, hyperuricemia) diagnose AFLP. (Book p408)

questions.q: What characteristic histopathological lesion is seen in maternal liver tissue in patients with AFLP?
opts: Microvesicular fatty infiltration / steatosis of hepatocytes with centrally placed nuclei, predominantly in zone 3
Macrovesicular steatosis with peripheral nuclear displacement
Hepatic granulomas with Langhans giant cells
questions.exp: AFLP is characterized by diffuse microvesicular steatosis where small fat droplets crowd the hepatocyte cytoplasm without displacing the nucleus. (Book p408)

questions.q: What is the definitive medical management for a pregnant woman diagnosed with Acute Fatty Liver of Pregnancy in the third trimester?
opts: Immediate maternal hemodynamic and metabolic stabilization followed by prompt delivery of the fetus regardless of gestational age
High-dose oral steroid therapy and discharge
questions.exp: AFLP is a medical emergency with up to 10% maternal mortality; prompt delivery halts the disease, with maternal liver function recovering within 1-2 weeks. (Book p408)

questions.q: What is the cardinal presenting symptom of Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy (ICP)?
opts: Generalized pruritus characteristically localized to the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, worsening significantly at night, WITHOUT primary skin lesions
A maculopapular erythematous rash starting on the periumbilical striae
Intense right lower quadrant rebound tenderness
Painful bullae on the extensor surfaces
questions.exp: ICP presents with nocturnal pruritus centered on palms and soles in the absence of primary skin lesions; skin excoriations may develop secondary to scratching. (Book p408)

questions.q: Why does maternal Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy carry an increased risk of maternal antepartum and postpartum hemorrhage?
opts: Decreased intestinal bile salts impair the micellar absorption of fat-soluble Vitamin K, leading to coagulopathy (prolonged PT/INR)
Direct platelet destruction by bile salts in the spleen
Massive consumption of fibrinogen in placental vessels
questions.exp: Cholestasis impairs intestinal fat-soluble vitamin absorption, specifically Vitamin K, leading to deficiency of factors II, VII, IX, and X, raising bleeding risk. (Book p408)

questions.q: What is the single most sensitive and specific diagnostic laboratory investigation for Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy?
opts: Total serum bile acid (SBA) level > 10 micromol/L
questions.exp: Fasting total serum bile acids > 10 micromol/L confirms ICP; levels >= 40 micromol/L indicate moderate-to-severe disease with heightened fetal danger. (Book p409)

questions.q: Why is Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy associated with sudden unexplained intrauterine fetal demise near term?
opts: High concentrations of maternal bile acids cross into the fetal circulation, inducing acute fetal cardiac dysrhythmias and sudden cardiac arrest
Bile salts trigger acute rupture of the umbilical cord
Placental abruption occurs in 100% of cases
questions.exp: Bile acids accumulate in fetal cardiomyocytes, causing calcium influx abnormalities, ventricular arrhythmias, bowel peristalsis (meconium), and sudden stillbirth. (Book p409)

questions.q: What is the medical DRUG OF CHOICE for symptomatic relief and biochemical improvement in Intrahepatic Cholestasis of Pregnancy?
opts: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 10 to 15 mg/kg/day orally PLUS Vitamin K supplementation
questions.exp: UDCA displaces toxic hydrophobic endogenous bile acids, restores hepatobiliary transport, relieves maternal pruritus, and improves liver biochemistry. (Book p409)

questions.q: On which human chromosome are the Rh blood group genes (RHD and RHCE) located?
questions.exp: The Rh genetic locus resides on the short arm of chromosome 1 (1p36.13-p34.3) and encodes the multi-pass transmembrane Rh antigens. (Book p410)

questions.q: At what gestational age do Rh antigens first appear on the surface of human fetal red blood cell membranes?
opts: By 38 days after fertilization (approximately 6 weeks of gestation)
Only after birth following first breath
questions.exp: Rh antigens are fully formed and immunogenic on embryonic erythrocytes as early as day 38 of embryonic development (~6 weeks GA). (Book p410)

questions.q: If an Rh-negative pregnant woman conceives with a husband who is heterozygous Rh-positive (Dd), what is the probability that the fetus will be Rh-positive?
opts: 50% chance of Rh-positive fetus (Dd) and 50% chance of Rh-negative fetus (dd)
questions.exp: With a heterozygous Rh-positive father (Dd) and Rh-negative mother (dd), Mendelian inheritance predicts 50% Dd (Rh-positive) and 50% dd (Rh-negative). (Book p410)

questions.q: Why is the FIRST pregnancy of an unsensitized Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus almost always unaffected by hemolytic disease of the newborn?
opts: The primary immune response predominantly produces IgM antibodies, which are pentameric and cannot cross the placenta; IgG antibodies are formed post-delivery
Fetal red cells do not have Rh antigens in the first pregnancy
Placental enzymes destroy all maternal antibodies
questions.exp: Primary immune response to feto-maternal hemorrhage during delivery generates IgM (MW 900 kDa), which cannot cross syncytiotrophoblasts; IgG develops later. (Book p411)

questions.q: In a subsequent pregnancy of an Rh-sensitized mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus, what antibody class crosses the placenta to cause fetal hemolysis?
opts: Maternal IgG Anti-D antibodies (actively transported across the placenta via FcRn receptors)
Maternal IgA antibodies from breast milk
questions.exp: Anamnestic memory response rapidly produces monomeric IgG anti-D, which crosses via placental neonatal Fc receptors (FcRn) to destroy fetal RBCs. (Book p411)

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism of fetal red blood cell destruction in Rh isoimmunization?
opts: Extravascular hemolysis in the fetal spleen by splenic macrophages recognizing IgG-coated fetal erythrocytes
Intravascular complement-mediated cell lysis in umbilical veins
Direct mechanical shearing against cardiac valves
questions.exp: IgG-coated fetal RBCs are phagocytosed extravascularly by fetal splenic reticuloendothelial macrophages, releasing indirect bilirubin. (Book p411)

questions.q: Why do fetuses with severe Rh isoimmunization develop prominent hepatosplenomegaly?
opts: Profound compensatory extramedullary hematopoiesis in the fetal liver and spleen in response to severe anemia
Direct storage of intact bilirubin crystals
Glycogen deposition stimulated by fetal insulin
questions.exp: Severe anemia drives intense compensatory extramedullary erythropoiesis in the fetal liver and spleen, causing marked organomegaly. (Book p412)

questions.q: What ultrasound finding is recognized as the earliest pathognomonic sign ('Buddha sign') of impending Hydrops Fetalis?
opts: Scalp subcutaneous edema appearing as a halo around the fetal cranium
questions.exp: Fetal scalp subcutaneous edema creates a double-contour appearance resembling the halo around Buddha's head ('Buddha sign'), the earliest sign of hydrops. (Book p412)

questions.q: What diagnostic ultrasound criteria confirm the clinical diagnosis of Hydrops Fetalis?
opts: Abnormal fluid accumulation in at least TWO fetal serous body compartments (ascites, pleural effusion, pericardial effusion, or generalized skin edema)
Single unilocular ovarian cyst in female fetus
questions.exp: Hydrops fetalis is defined sonographically by pathological fluid accumulation in at least two serous cavities or one cavity plus diffuse anasarca. (Book p412)

questions.q: What classic fetal heart rate pattern on cardiotocography (CTG) is indicative of severe fetal anemia and tissue hypoxia?
opts: Sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern (smooth, undulating wave with frequency of 2-5 cycles/min and amplitude 5-15 bpm)
questions.exp: A true sinusoidal FHR pattern is an ominous Category III tracing indicating profound fetal anemia (erythroblastosis) or severe hypoxia. (Book p412)

questions.q: What laboratory test is performed on MATERNAL venous blood to determine whether an Rh-negative pregnant woman is already sensitized?
opts: Indirect Coombs Test (ICT) / Indirect Antiglobulin Test
questions.exp: The Indirect Coombs Test detects circulating maternal IgG anti-D antibodies in maternal serum; a negative test confirms the mother is unsensitized. (Book p412)

questions.q: At what gestational age is routine antenatal Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis administered to an unsensitized Rh-negative pregnant woman?
opts: At 28 weeks of gestation (single dose of 300 mcg / 1500 IU IM)
questions.exp: Routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis is given at 28 weeks (300 mcg / 1500 IU) because fetomaternal hemorrhages naturally increase in the third trimester. (Book p413)

questions.q: Following the delivery of an Rh-positive infant, within what ideal timeframe should the Rh-negative mother receive postpartum Anti-D immunoglobulin?
opts: Within 72 hours of delivery (can still provide partial benefit if given up to 28 days postpartum)
questions.exp: Postpartum anti-D should be administered ideally within 72 hours of delivery; if missed, it can be given up to 28 days post-delivery. (Book p413)

questions.q: What umbilical cord management strategy is recommended during the delivery of an Rh-negative unsensitized mother?
opts: Early umbilical cord clamping, to minimize fetomaternal transfusion of fetal red cells into maternal circulation
Milking the cord toward the fetus five times
questions.exp: Early cord clamping in unsensitized Rh-negative mothers minimizes fetomaternal microtransfusion at delivery, reducing the risk of sensitization. (Book p413)

questions.q: In an Rh-negative sensitized pregnant woman (ICT positive), what maternal antibody titer is recognized as the CRITICAL TITER requiring initiation of fetal surveillance for anemia?
questions.exp: A critical antibody titer of >= 1:16 (or 1:32) indicates sufficient antibody load to cause hydrops fetalis, mandating Doppler surveillance. (Book p414)

questions.q: What is the non-invasive screening investigation of choice to detect and monitor fetal anemia in an Rh-sensitized pregnancy?
opts: Doppler measurement of Middle Cerebral Artery Peak Systolic Velocity (MCA PSV)
questions.exp: MCA PSV Doppler (Mari criteria) is the non-invasive gold standard; reduced fetal blood viscosity and hyperdynamic circulation increase peak systolic velocity. (Book p414)

questions.q: What Middle Cerebral Artery Peak Systolic Velocity (MCA PSV) threshold indicates moderate-to-severe fetal anemia?
opts: MCA PSV >= 1.5 Multiples of the Median (MoM)
questions.exp: An MCA PSV >= 1.5 MoM indicates moderate to severe fetal anemia with >95% sensitivity, prompting diagnostic cordocentesis and transfusion. (Book p414)

questions.q: When severe fetal anemia (hematocrit < 30%) is confirmed via cordocentesis in a fetus at 28 weeks of gestation, what is the definitive therapeutic intervention?
opts: Intrauterine Blood Transfusion (IUT) into the umbilical vein using fresh, irradiated, CMV-negative, O Rh-negative packed red blood cells
questions.exp: IUT into the umbilical vein with O-negative irradiated CMV-negative PRBCs corrects severe fetal anemia and reverses hydrops until term is reached. (Book p415)

questions.q: At what gestational age is planned delivery indicated for an Rh-sensitized pregnancy that has reached near-term maturity or after successful IUT stabilization?
questions.exp: Delivery is planned at 37-38 weeks once fetal maturity is reached to avoid late intrauterine fetal demise while minimizing neonatal prematurity risks. (Book p415)

questions.q: A standard prophylactic single vial of 300 mcg (1500 IU) Anti-D immunoglobulin covers what volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage?
opts: Up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood (or 15 mL of fetal packed red blood cells)
Up to 5 mL of fetal whole blood
Up to 100 mL of fetal whole blood
Up to 300 mL of fetal whole blood
questions.exp: Standard 300 mcg anti-D neutralizes up to 30 mL of fetal whole blood (equivalent to 15 mL of packed fetal RBCs). (Book p415)

questions.q: What laboratory test is used to quantitatively calculate the exact volume of fetomaternal hemorrhage in maternal blood based on the acid resistance of fetal hemoglobin?
questions.exp: Kleihauer-Betke test exploits the acid resistance of fetal hemoglobin (HbF); adult RBCs elute hemoglobin leaving ghost cells, allowing precise fetal RBC counting. (Book p416)

questions.q: For every additional 1 mL of fetal whole blood detected in maternal circulation beyond the baseline 30 mL, how much additional Anti-D immunoglobulin must be administered?
questions.exp: Additional anti-D dosing: 10 mcg per 1 mL of additional fetal whole blood (or 20 mcg per 1 mL of fetal packed red blood cells). (Book p416)

questions.q: Which minor red blood cell antigen is the MOST COMMON cause of maternal alloimmunization following a mismatched blood transfusion, uniquely causing erythroid precursor suppression in addition to hemolysis?
questions.exp: Anti-Kell antibodies not only cause hemolysis but also destroy early erythroid progenitor cells in fetal bone marrow, causing rapid and severe anemia. (Book p417)

questions.q: What rare condition, also known as Ballantyne syndrome, is characterized by generalized maternal edema and pre-eclampsia-like features mirroring severe fetal hydrops?
questions.exp: Mirror syndrome (maternal hydrops mirroring fetal hydrops) features generalized maternal edema and placental enlargement accompanying hydrops fetalis. (Book p417)
